newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pope pins hopes on young people to boost religion.
newsitem.headline: Pope pins hopes on young people to boost religion.

text.p: Pope John Paul, preparing to preside over a Roman Catholic world youth festival in Paris this week, has called on young people to shake the West out of growing religious indifference and egoism.
The pope, in a rare written interview with the French daily La Croix, published on Tuesday, described young people as "witnesses of hope", praising their generosity, enthusiasm and idealism.
"I know that the Church in France as elsewhere, especially in the West, is going through a decline in religious practice and in religious and priesthood vocations," he said.
"In a few days, young people from the five continents will know how to let you see what they expect from you, France's catholics," he said.
The 77-year-old pontiff is due in Paris on Thursday for a four-day visit culminating with a vast open-air mass at the Longchamp race course on the capital's western outskirts.

"I expect young people to mobilise their generosity, intelligence and energy to make a world more hospitable for all, to dedicate themselves to the happiness and dignity of their brothers and sisters," he said.

French church officials fear that the turnout for the 12th World Youth Days celebration could be embarrassingly low. They had initially hoped that 600,000 "young people" -- defined as aged between 17 and 35 -- would flock.
They admitted last week that far fewer than forecast had signed up to attend the celebrations, fewer families had come forward to host them and fund-raising had also been a problem.

But the chief organiser, Bishop Michel Dubost, was upbeat on Monday, saying many French pilgrims had registered late. He told reporters 160 countries would be represented, and the number of pilgrims would easily reach 350,000.
Police said about 300,000 people attended a mass on Tuesday opening the youth celebrations, celebrated at the Eiffel Tower by Paris Archbishop Jean-Marie Lustiger.
In once fervently Catholic France, only six million attend mass regularly and many ignore or oppose the Pope's strict moral teachings and bans on abortion, contraception and homosexuality.
The Pope is expected to use his sixth trip to France to focus on social justice and urge the young to shun material temptations and live more wholesome, spiritual lives.

But he has been loudly criticised by leftist and family planning groups over plans to pay a private visit to the grave of his geneticist friend Jerome Lejeune, a staunch anti-abortion campaigner who is said to have inspired his teachings.

French Protestants are also upset that the Sunday climax of the visit, a mass the Church hopes will draw half a million people, falls on the anniversary of the St Bartholemew's Day massacre of up to 70,000 Huguenots by Catholic forces in 1572.

Perhaps in a reference to the massacre, the Pope told La Croix that the Christian world had seen in the past millenium "painful conflicts in open opposition to the will of Christ that are a cause of scandal for the world".
